segments.translit: tam evā[rthaṃ] paramakaruṇāmreḍitasiddhācāryyo hi ḍombī| naukāpravāhavyājena prakaṭayati—
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Ḍombī]{p-dombi}, moved again and again by supreme compassion, makes that same point plain under the guise of rowing a [boat]{boat}:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as the work of the siddha master Ḍombī, who, moved again and again by supreme compassion, sets out ‘that same point’ under the guise of rowing a boat. The phrase refers back to his preceding comment.

flags.note: paramakaruṇāmreḍita: āmreḍita literally means ‘repeated, reiterated’. I rendered ‘moved again and again by supreme compassion’; ‘filled with’ or ‘steeped in’ supreme compassion is also possible.
tam evārtham (‘that same point’) refers back to the comment on the previous song, which is outside this pack. Shastri's restoration [rthaṃ] is needed for the sense and I translated through it.
The poet is named here simply ḍombī, without -pāda. I kept the surface ‘Ḍombī’ and linked it to p-dombi, whose approved English is ‘Ḍombīpāda’ (see questions).

segments.translit:
gaṅgetyādi| gaṅgāyamuneti sandhyayā candrābhāsasūryyābhāsau grāhyagrāhakau| yasyā[ḥ] śukranāḍikā viramānandāva[22ka]dhūtikāyā madhye varttate| sā eva nauḥ sandhyābhāṣayā boddhavyā|
sadguru ityādi vilakṣaṇaśuddhā| tatra sthitvā sahajayānapramattāṅgī ḍombī nairātmā saṃsārārṇave yogīndra[ḥ] pāraṃ karotīti|
segments.translation: ‘[Gaṅgā]{pl-ganga}’ and so on. The [Gaṅgā]{pl-ganga} and the [Yamunā]{pl-yamuna} are, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, the [moon]{moon}-[appearance]{abhasa} and the [sun]{surya}-[appearance]{abhasa}, [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka}. The [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, in the middle of which the channel of semen runs: that is what is to be understood, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, as the [boat]{boat}. ‘The true [guru]{guru}’ and so on: purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}. Staying there, [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, her body drunk with the vehicle of the [innate]{sahaja}, takes the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} [across]{para} the ocean of [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, in twilight language, as the moon-appearance and the sun-appearance, the grasped and the grasper. The boat is the avadhūtī (the central channel) of the joy of cessation, in which the channel of semen runs. Ḍombī, Nairātmā (selflessness as a goddess), intoxicated with the innate vehicle, ferries the lord of yogis across saṃsāra's ocean.

equations.en: the moon-appearance (candrābhāsa), the grasped; the pairing follows word order only
the sun-appearance (sūryābhāsa), the grasper; the pairing follows word order only
the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation, in the middle of which the channel of semen (śukranāḍikā) runs; the syntax also allows the channel itself
Nairātmā (in apposition, standing where the song has the Mātaṅgī)

flags.note: yasyāḥ … viramānandāvadhūtikāyā madhye … sā eva nauḥ: I take the feminine relative yasyāḥ with avadhūtikāyāḥ, so that sā, the boat, is the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation within which the channel of semen runs. The syntax also lets sā pick up śukranāḍikā, which would make the channel of semen itself the boat. The glossary's boat entry currently reads it that way.

sadguru ityādi is out of place here. The refrain (sadguru …) is commented on in cp.14.m3, and what follows paraphrases line 1b (tahiṃ → tatra; pāra karei → pāraṃ karoti). vilakṣaṇaśuddhā is feminine and most likely qualifies the boat (nauḥ) of the preceding sentence. The lemma may be misplaced or miscopied (for tahiṃ ityādi?). Translated as printed.

yogīndra[ḥ]: Shastri restores a nominative visarga, but the sense (Ḍombī takes the lord of yogis across, as the Mātaṅgī ferries the young one in the song) needs the accusative yogīndra[ṃ]. I translated it as the object.

sahajayānapramattāṅgī ‘her body drunk with the vehicle of the innate’: pramatta (‘intoxicated’) would sit more naturally with sahajapāna (‘drinking of the innate’), and yāna and pāna are easily confused. Translated as printed.

In his paraphrase of 1b Munidatta puts Ḍombī, Nairātmā where the song has the Mātaṅgī, and the lord of yogis where it has poiālī (the draft's ‘young one’). pramattāṅgī (‘drunk-bodied’) and sthitvā (‘staying’) may answer the song's buṛilī (the draft's ‘immersed’). None of these is an explicit ‘X iti Y’ gloss. Of them I list only the apposition ḍombī = Nairātmā in equations.
Munidatta writes avadhūtikā; I used the approved English ‘avadhūtī’ (avadhuti). candrābhāsa/sūryābhāsa are linked to moon/sun and to the proposed entry abhasa.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena pratyayasandarśanāt| kulābhyāsaṃ kurute—
bāhutu ityādi| sahajaśodhitaviramānandanaumārge prāpte sati khānapānāśaktitvena bho ḍombi ātmānaṃ saṃbo[dhya] vadati kimarthaṃ vilamba[ḥ] kriyate| sadgurusaṃbodhyena nirantarābhyāsena punar jinapuraṃ mahāsukhapuraṃ atīva sannihitaṃ| evaṃ anucintyānudina[ṃ] pravāham abhyāsaṃ kuru|
segments.translation: By the [refrain]{dhruvapada}, because it shows grounds for confidence, he undertakes the kula practice: ‘Row’ and so on. When the [boat]{boat}-path of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, purified by the [innate]{sahaja}, has been reached, owing to attachment to eating and drinking he addresses himself, ‘O [Ḍombī]{dombi}’, and says, ‘Why is there delay?’ Through the true [guru]{guru}'s instruction and unbroken practice, the [city of the Jina]{jinapura}, the city of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, is once again very near. Reflecting in this way, practise the rowing day after day.
segments.note: Munidatta hears the refrain as the singer addressing himself, ‘O Ḍombī’, on account of attachment to eating and drinking: the boat-path of the joy of cessation, purified by the innate, has been reached, so why delay? Through the true guru's instruction and unbroken practice the city of the Jina, the city of great bliss, is very near; practise daily.

flags.note: dhruvapadena pratyayasandarśanāt | kulābhyāsaṃ kurute: the sense of kulābhyāsa is unclear, and I left kula untranslated. Possibilities: (a) kula ‘family, lineage’, a practice of the (tantric) family; (b) kūla ‘shore’, which the manuscript writes kula elsewhere (5b, cp.14.m6), i.e. practice aimed at the far shore; (c) a corruption, e.g. bahulābhyāsa ‘much practice’, which would suit the stress on constant practice that follows. The subject of kurute (the poet or the yogin) is also unstated.

bho ḍombi ātmānaṃ saṃbodhya vadati: literally ‘addressing himself, “O Ḍombī”, he says’. The poet is himself called Ḍombī, so Munidatta may take the refrain's vocative as the poet's self-address. saṃbodhya can also mean ‘rousing’ (himself). This sits awkwardly with cp.14.m2 and m6, where Ḍombī is Nairātmā the ferrywoman. I linked the vocative to dombi to match the draft of 2a; p-dombi is arguable.

khānapānāśaktitvena: read as āsakti ‘attachment’ (ś for s is common), hence ‘owing to attachment to eating and drinking’. If aśakti (‘inability’) is meant, the sense would be ‘through lack of strength for eating and drinking’.
sadgurusaṃbodhyena: saṃbodhya is a gerundive or absolutive, not a noun; saṃbodhena (‘instruction, awakening’) is probably meant. Translated ‘the true guru's instruction’.

pravāham abhyāsaṃ kuru: pravāha here and in cp.14.m4 seems to render the song's bāha- ‘row’, so ‘practise the rowing’. It could also mean ‘practise in a steady stream’. The lemma bāhutu is the song's bāhatu.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsasyānuśaṃsām āhuḥ—
pañcetyādi| pañcakeṛuālam iti| pañcakramopadeśaṃ gṛhītvā kacchikāmaṇimūlaṃ gataṃ, tad eva bodhicittaṃ sahajānandena vivṛtaṃ sad vaimalyaṃ cakroddeśena pravāhaṃ kuru| gaganadukholakaṃ caturthābhiṣekeṇa sicyamānaṃ yogīndrasya kāye pānīyaṃ viṣayollolanaṃ viśati|
segments.translation: In the second stanza he speaks of the benefit of practice: ‘Five’ and so on. ‘Five [oars]{keruala}’: having taken up the instruction of the [five stages]{pancakrama}, row by way of the wheels what has gone to the kacchikā, the [root of the jewel]{manimula}: that very [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, opened by [innate joy]{sahajananda} and become stainless. As the [sky]{gagana}-scoop is poured through the fourth [empowerment]{abhiseka}, the water, the surging of sense objects, enters the body of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}.
segments.note: Munidatta says this stanza shows the benefit of practice. The five oars are taking up the instruction of the five stages; bodhicitta, gone to the root of the jewel and opened by innate joy, is to be rowed by way of the wheels. He links the sky-scoop with the fourth empowerment and calls the water the surging of sense objects.

equations.en: taking up the instruction of the five stages (pañcakramopadeśa)
the root of the jewel (maṇimūla), if the compound kacchikāmaṇimūla is appositional

flags.note: pānīyaṃ viṣayollolanaṃ viśati ‘the water … enters’: the song (3b) says the water does not get in (na paisai). A na may have dropped out (viṣayollolanaṃ na viśati). Or Munidatta may mean that water poured through the fourth empowerment (abhiṣeka is literally ‘sprinkling’) does enter the body. Translated as printed and not harmonized with the draft.

kacchikāmaṇimūlaṃ gataṃ: I take kacchikā (the song's kācchī, ‘rope’ in the draft) as in apposition to maṇimūla, ‘the root of the jewel’, and gataṃ as agreeing with bodhicittaṃ. kacchikā could also name a place (‘the root of the jewel at the kacchikā’). I left kacchikā untranslated for that reason.
sad vaimalyaṃ: vaimalya is a noun (‘stainlessness’); I read it as if vimalaṃ, ‘become stainless’.
gaganadukholakaṃ … sicyamānaṃ has no finite verb; I take it as an absolute clause (‘as the sky-scoop is poured’). It may instead be a lemma followed by its gloss (‘the sky-scoop: being poured …’).
cakroddeśena: ‘by way of the wheels’ (the wheels of the subtle body), possibly ‘toward the wheel’. Not linked to the glossary's ‘wheel’, which is the image of 4a.
Munidatta calls couplet 3 the second stanza, 4 the third and 5 the fourth. He therefore counts couplet 1 as the first and leaves the refrain out of the count (see questions).

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadenābhyāsaviśeṣād ābhāṣa[23]trayanirodham āhu[ḥ]—
cāndetyādi| candraṃ prajñājñānaṃ sūryyam utpādād advayajñānaṃ pulindaṃ sandhyābhāṣayā napuṃsakaṃ| traya ete saṃsārasya sṛṣṭisaṃhārakārakāḥ| sarvvadharmmānupalambhajaladhau gacchan san vāmadakṣiṇam agrapaścāt tīram anupaśyantīti bho ḍombi svacchandena vilakṣaṇaśodhitaṣodhicittanauvāhanābhyāsaṃ kuru|
segments.translation: In the third stanza he speaks of stopping the three [appearances]{abhasa} through a special practice: ‘[Moon]{moon}’ and so on. The [moon]{moon} is the knowledge of wisdom; the [sun]{surya}, from arising; nondual knowledge, the [pulinda]{pulinda}, is in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} the neuter. These three bring about the [creation and destruction]{srsti-samhara} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}. Going on the ocean where no phenomenon is apprehended, they look to the shore left and right, ahead and behind. O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, as you please, practise rowing the [boat]{boat} of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}.
segments.note: Munidatta says this stanza teaches how a special practice stops the three appearances. The moon is the knowledge of wisdom, the pulinda in twilight language ‘the neuter’ (the sun's gloss seems corrupt). These three make and unmake saṃsāra. On the ocean where nothing is apprehended, Ḍombī is told to practise freely rowing the boat of bodhicitta purified by vilakṣaṇa.

equations.en: unclear as printed: ‘from arising’ (utpādāt); perhaps originally the knowledge of means (upāyajñāna)
in twilight language, the neuter (napuṃsaka); probably also nondual knowledge (advayajñāna)
bodhicitta purified by vilakṣaṇa (‘the boat of bodhicitta’)

flags.note: sūryam utpādād advayajñānaṃ: the gloss on the sun is incomplete or corrupt. The pairing with prajñājñāna leads one to expect upāyajñānam (‘the knowledge of means’). I translated literally (‘the sun, from arising’) and took advayajñānam (‘nondual knowledge’) with the pulinda, which suits the neuter as a third term uniting the two. It could instead belong to the sun (‘the sun, from arising, is nondual knowledge’).

tīram anupaśyantīti ‘they look to the shore’: the song (4b) says ‘not looking’ (na rebai). Either a na has dropped out (tīraṃ nānupaśyanti) or Munidatta's sense differs; not harmonized. The subject is also unclear: gacchan san is masculine singular, anupaśyanti plural.
ṣodhicitta is a misprint or miscopying for bodhicitta (ষ for ব); translated as bodhicitta.
ābhāṣa is ābhāsa, ‘appearance’; I propose an entry (abhasa). vilakṣaṇaśodhita may be ‘purified by vilakṣaṇa’ (the fourth moment) or simply ‘extraordinarily purified’ (see the vilaksana proposal).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena nairātmadharmmasya phalānuśaṃsām āhu[ḥ]—
kabaḍītyādi| yathā bāhye pārāvāre tarapatis tarakaparddikāṃ gṛhṇāti| tadvad grāhyagrāhakatayā sā bhagavatī ḍombī nairātmā na pratigṛhṇāti| artha paricaryyāmātreṇāgrāhyatayā bhavasamudre pāraṃ karotīti| nairātnadharmmāparicayena bahiḥśāstrābhimānino ye yoginas te 'pi kule śarīre bhramantīti ajñānenāvṛtā bālā ityādi| 14||
segments.translation: In the fourth stanza he speaks of the benefit that the teaching of [selflessness]{nairatmya} yields as its fruit: ‘[Cowrie]{kabadi}’ and so on. Just as in the outer world the ferry-master at a crossing takes a [cowrie]{kabadi} as the fare, the blessed lady [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, does not accept in that way, in the manner of [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka}. Rather, with service alone, being beyond grasping, she ferries [across]{para} the ocean of becoming. Those yogis who, unacquainted with the teaching of [selflessness]{nairatmya}, pride themselves on outer treatises: they too wander on the [shore]{kula-shore}, that is, in the body. ‘Fools veiled by ignorance…’ and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta contrasts the ordinary ferry-master, who takes a cowrie as fare, with the blessed Ḍombī, Nairātmā, who accepts nothing as grasped and grasper and ferries across the ocean of becoming for service alone. The shore where others sink he reads as the body, in which yogis proud of outer treatises, unfamiliar with selflessness, wander.

citations.quoted: ajñānenāvṛtā bālā ityādi (‘Fools veiled by ignorance…’ and so on)

flags.note: artha paricaryāmātreṇa: artha makes no sense as printed; probably atha (‘rather, but’) or arthāt (‘that is to say’). Translated ‘Rather’.
nairātmadharma: the glossary lists this form under nairatma (the goddess), but here it plainly means the teaching (or nature) of selflessness, so I linked ‘selflessness’ (nairatmya) in both places.

paricaryāmātreṇa ‘with service alone’: she takes no fare beyond the yogin's attendance on her. paricaryā (‘service’) is not the glossary's caryā (‘conduct’), despite the automatic hit, and is not linked.
nairātna- is a misprint for nairātma-.

Munidatta does not explicitly gloss ‘those who climbed onto a chariot’ (5b); in his paraphrase the yogis proud of outer treatises stand in their place. tadvad … na pratigṛhṇāti is read as ‘does not accept in that way’ (a contrast with the ferry-master), not ‘likewise does not accept’.
The closing ‘14||’ is the song number, not Munidatta's wording, and is not translated.

proposals.definition: Appearance or luminosity. Munidatta pairs a moon-appearance and a sun-appearance, which he equates with the grasped and the grasper (cp.14.m2), and speaks of three appearances, the moon, the sun and the pulinda, which make and unmake saṃsāra and which practice stops (cp.14.m5).
proposals.rationale: Occurs twice in this commentary (spelled ābhāsa and ābhāṣa). At present it is described only inside the moon, sun and pulinda entries. The triad with a ‘neuter’ third looks like the three appearances of Guhyasamāja completion-stage teaching. The reviewer may want to check that link before the entry says so.

proposals.definition: ‘Beyond characteristics’: in the Hevajra system, the last of the four moments (kṣaṇa) of yogic union, commonly paired with innate joy, though systems differ. Munidatta twice speaks of something ‘purified by vilakṣaṇa’: the boat or the avadhūtī (cp.14.m2), and the bodhicitta that is rowed as a boat (cp.14.m5).
proposals.rationale: Recurs in cp.14.m2 and cp.14.m5 and parallels ‘purified by the innate’ (sahajaśodhita) in cp.14.m3, which points to the technical sense rather than the ordinary adjective ‘distinctive, extraordinary’. If the reviewer prefers the ordinary sense, no entry is needed and both phrases can read ‘extraordinarily pure(d)’.

proposals.definition: ‘Root of the jewel’: a point in the lower body named in the code language of the yoginī tantras, where the ‘jewel’ (maṇi) usually stands for the male organ. Munidatta says bodhicitta goes to the kacchikā, the root of the jewel, and, opened by innate joy, is to be rowed by way of the wheels (cp.14.m4).
proposals.rationale: The viramananda entry already mentions maṇimūla, so the term seems to recur in the commentary, and an entry lets the woven notes link it. The anatomical gloss in the definition reflects common tantric usage; the reviewer should check it.

questions: p-dombi: in cp.14.m1 the poet is called only ḍombī. I linked the surface ‘Ḍombī’ to p-dombi (approved English ‘Ḍombīpāda’). Should the entry list ‘Ḍombī’ as a variant, or should the commentary read ‘Ḍombīpāda’?

cp.14.m3: Munidatta seems to take the refrain's ‘O Ḍombī’ as the poet addressing (or rousing) himself (ātmānaṃ saṃbodhya). Link it to p-dombi or to dombi (I used dombi)? And should the dombi entry record this reading beside the Nairātmā one?

boat entry: the grammar of cp.14.m2 (yasyāḥ … avadhūtikāyāḥ … sā) favours the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation as the boat, with the channel of semen inside it. The entry currently says the channel. Revise?
matangi entry says its reading is unattested, but in cp.14.m2 Munidatta's paraphrase of 1b puts ‘Ḍombī, Nairātmā’ where the song has the Mātaṅgī. Record this as an implicit reading?
Draft 1b ‘immersed’ (buṛilī): Munidatta seems to answer it with ‘staying there’ and pramattāṅgī ‘drunk-bodied’. Is that worth a note on the line?

Draft 3b and 4b have negations (the water does not get in; not looking left and right), but the printed commentary has none (viśati, cp.14.m4; anupaśyanti, cp.14.m5). Can the manuscript or the Tibetan (toh2293) be checked for a lost na?
nairātmadharma (cp.14.m6) is listed as a form of nairatma. I linked it to nairatmya (selflessness). Move the form?
The automatic glossary hits contain false matches: carya for paricaryā ‘service’ (cp.14.m6), and citta inside bodhicitta/ṣodhicitta (cp.14.m4, m5). I did not link them.

Stanza numbering: Munidatta calls couplets 3–5 the second to fourth stanzas, i.e. he counts couplet 1 as the first and leaves the refrain out. The text brief says he counts from the couplet after the refrain. Should the brief be corrected?

kācchī (3a, draft ‘rope’): Munidatta renders it kacchikā and apparently equates it with the root of the jewel. Should kācchī get its own entry carrying that reading? I left kacchikā untranslated in cp.14.m4.
cp.14.m3 kulābhyāsa: I left kula untranslated (family? shore? corruption?). Please decide the rendering.
The quotation ‘ajñānenāvṛtā bālāḥ …’ (cp.14.m6) is unidentified; can you trace it?
